Abstract.

We derive modular parametrizations for certain infinite series whose summands involve central binomial coefficients and higher-order harmonic numbers. When the rates of convergence are certain rational numbers, modularity allows us to reduce the corresponding series to special values of the Dirichlet LL-functions. For example, we establish the following identities conjectured by Sun:

∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−2592​𝖧k(2)+735​L−7​(2)−86​π21104]​14096k=0,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{25}{92}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}+\frac{735L_{-7}(2)-86\pi^{2}}{1104}\right]\frac{1}{4096^{k}}=0,
∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(3)−43352​𝖧k(3)]​42​k+54096k=555​ζ​(3)77​π−32​G11,\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(3)}-\frac{43}{352}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(3)}\right]\frac{42k+5}{4096^{k}}=\frac{555\zeta(3)}{77\pi}-\frac{32G}{11},

where 𝖧(r)k:⁣=∑0<n≤k1nr\mathsf{H}^{(r)}_{k}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{0<n\leq k}\frac{1}{n^{r}}, L−7(2):⁣=∑n=1∞(−7n)1n2=112+122−132+142−152−162+182+⋯L_{-7}(2)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{-7}{n}\right)\frac{1}{n^{2}}=\frac{1}{1^{2}}+\frac{1}{2^{2}}-\frac{1}{3^{2}}+\frac{1}{4^{2}}-\frac{1}{5^{2}}-\frac{1}{6^{2}}+\frac{1}{8^{2}}+\cdots, G:⁣=∑n=0∞(−1)n(2​n+1)2G\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{n}}{(2n+1)^{2}}, and ζ(3):⁣=∑n=1∞1n3\zeta(3)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{3}}.

1. Introduction

The four known classical rational Ramanujan-type series (see [32, Chapter 14]) involving cubes of central binomial coefficients (2​kk):⁣=(2​k)!(k!)2\binom{2k}{k}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\frac{(2k)!}{(k!)^{2}} are

(1.1) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​4​k+1(−64)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\frac{4k+1}{(-64)^{k}} =2π,\displaystyle=\frac{2}{\pi},
(1.2) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​6​k+1256k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\frac{6k+1}{256^{k}} =4π,\displaystyle=\frac{4}{\pi},
(1.3) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​6​k+1(−512)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\frac{6k+1}{(-512)^{k}} =2​2π,\displaystyle=\frac{2\sqrt{2}}{\pi},
(1.4) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​42​k+54096k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\frac{42k+5}{4096^{k}} =16π.\displaystyle=\frac{16}{\pi}.

Note that (1.1) was first obtained by Bauer [13], and (1.2)–(1.4) were discovered by Ramanujan [52]. Usually, one proves such identities using the theory of modular forms (see, for example, [43, 51, 59]). The identities (1.1)–(1.4) have the following variants involving second-order harmonic numbers 𝖧(2)k:⁣=∑0<n≤k1n2\mathsf{H}^{(2)}_{k}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{0<n\leq k}\frac{1}{n^{2}}:

(1.5) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−12​𝖧k(2)]​4​k+1(−64)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}\right]\frac{4k+1}{(-64)^{k}} =−π12,\displaystyle=-\frac{\pi}{12},
(1.6) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−516​𝖧k(2)]​6​k+1256k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{5}{16}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}\right]\frac{6k+1}{256^{k}} =π12,\displaystyle=\frac{\pi}{12},
(1.7) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−516​𝖧k(2)]​6​k+1(−512)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{5}{16}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}\right]\frac{6k+1}{(-512)^{k}} =−2​π48,\displaystyle=-\frac{\sqrt{2}\pi}{48},
(1.8) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−2592​𝖧k(2)]​42​k+54096k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{25}{92}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}\right]\frac{42k+5}{4096^{k}} =2​π69.\displaystyle=\frac{2\pi}{69}.

Here is a brief history of the last four displayed formulae: Wei and Ruan [64] established (1.5); Guo and Lian [42] had conjectured (1.6) and (1.7) before both formulae were confirmed by Wei [62]; Sun [55, (107)] had proposed (1.8) before it was verified by Wei [60].

Motivated by the identities (1.5)–(1.8), the first-named author has recently conjectured the following four identities (cf. [56]):

(1.9) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−12​𝖧k(2)+2​L−8​(2)−5​π224]​1(−64)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{1}{2}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}+2L_{-8}(2)-\frac{5\pi^{2}}{24}\right]\frac{1}{(-64)^{k}} =0,\displaystyle=0,
(1.10) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−516​𝖧k(2)+135​L−3​(2)−11​π296]​1256k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{5}{16}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}+\frac{135L_{-3}(2)-11\pi^{2}}{96}\right]\frac{1}{256^{k}} =0,\displaystyle=0,
(1.11) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−516​𝖧k(2)+120​L−4​(2)−11​π296]​1(−512)k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{5}{16}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}+\frac{120L_{-4}(2)-11\pi^{2}}{96}\right]\frac{1}{(-512)^{k}} =0,\displaystyle=0,
(1.12) ∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−2592​𝖧k(2)+735​L−7​(2)−86​π21104]​14096k\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{25}{92}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}+\frac{735L_{-7}(2)-86\pi^{2}}{1104}\right]\frac{1}{4096^{k}} =0.\displaystyle=0.

Here, the Dirichlet LL-function

(1.13) Ld(s):⁣=∑n=1∞(dn)1ns,Res>1\displaystyle L_{d}(s)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\left(\frac{d}{n}\right)\frac{1}{n^{s}},\quad\RE s>1

is defined via the Kronecker symbol (d⋅)\big(\frac{d}{\cdot}\big). The Riemann zeta function

(1.14) ζ(s):⁣=∑n=1∞1ns,Res>1\displaystyle\zeta(s)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{n^{s}},\quad\RE s>1

is the same as L1​(s)L_{1}(s).

To attack (1.9)–(1.12) and to revisit (1.5)–(1.8) in §2, we give modular parametrizations for our series of interest. We will need the Dedekind eta function η(z):⁣=eπ​i​z/12∏n=1∞(1−e2​π​i​n​z)\eta(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}e^{\pi iz/12}\prod_{n=1}^{\infty}(1-e^{2\pi inz}) for z∈ℌ:⁣={𝔴∈ℭ|Im𝔴>0}z\in\mathfrak H\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\{w\in\mathbb C|\I w>0\}, from which we may define the modular lambda function

(1.15) λ(2z)≡α4(z):⁣=24​[η⁡(z)]8​[η⁡(4​z)]16[η⁡(2​z)]24=1−α4(−14​z)=1−λ(−12​z)\displaystyle\lambda(2z)\equiv\alpha_{4}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\frac{2^{4}[\eta(z)]^{8}[\eta(4z)]^{16}}{[\eta(2z)]^{24}}=1-\alpha_{4}\left(-\frac{1}{4z}\right)=1-\lambda\left(-\frac{1}{2z}\right)

and the weight-4 holomorphic Eisenstein series

(1.16) E4(z):⁣=\displaystyle E_{4}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}{} [η⁡(z)]40​{1−λ⁡(z)+[λ⁡(z)]2}[η⁡(2​z)​η​(z/2)]16=12​ζ​(4)​∑m,n∈Zm2+n2≠01(m​z+n)4=1+240​∑n=1∞⁡n3​e2​π​i​n​z1−e2​π​i​n​z\displaystyle\frac{[\eta(z)]^{40}\{1-\lambda(z)+[\lambda(z)]^{2}\}}{[\eta(2z)\eta(z/2)]^{16}}=\frac{1}{2\zeta(4)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb Z\\ m^{2}+n^{2}\neq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{(mz+n)^{4}}=1+240\mathop{\raisebox{-10.00012pt}{\scalebox{1.0}{$\displaystyle\sum$}}}\limits_{n=1}^{\infty}\dfrac{n^{3}e^{2\pi inz}}{1-e^{2\pi inz}}

for z∈ℌz\in\mathfrak H. In addition, we will avail ourselves of the Eichler integral

(1.17) E4(z):⁣=∫zi​∞[1−E4(w)](w−z)2dw,\displaystyle E_{4}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\int_{z}^{i\infty}[1-E_{4}(w)](w-z)^{2}\D w,

the real-analytic Eisenstein series (also known as the Epstein zeta function)

(1.18) E(z,s):⁣=12​ζ​(2​s)∑m,n∈Zm2+n2≠0(Im⁡z)s|m​z+n|2​s=E(z+1,s)=E(−1z,s),\displaystyle E(z,s)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\frac{1}{2\zeta(2s)}\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}m,n\in\mathbb Z\\ m^{2}+n^{2}\neq 0\end{subarray}}\frac{(\I z)^{s}}{|mz+n|^{2s}}=E(z+1,s)=E\left(-\frac{1}{z},s\right),

the weight-2 non-holomorphic Eisenstein series

(1.19) E2(z):⁣=12π​i​η​(z)∂η⁡(z)∂z−3π​Im⁡z=1−3π​Im⁡z−24∑n=1∞n​e2​π​i​n​z1−e2​π​i​n​z,\displaystyle E_{2}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\frac{12}{\pi i\eta(z)}\frac{\partial\eta(z)}{\partial z}-\frac{3}{\pi\I z}=1-{\frac{3}{\pi\I z}-24\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{ne^{2\pi inz}}{1-e^{2\pi inz}}},

and the Legendre–Ramanujan function (cf. [71, (2.2.21)])

(1.20) R−1/2(1−2α4(z))=\displaystyle R_{-1/2}(1-2\alpha_{4}(z))={} −24​[E2​(4​z)]2−24​E4​(4​z)−[E2​(z)]2+E4​(z)2​[4​E2​(4​z)−E2​(z)]2.\displaystyle-\frac{2^{4}[E_{2}(4z)]^{2}-2^{4}E_{4}(4z)-[E_{2}(z)]^{2}+E_{4}(z)}{2[4E_{2}(4z)-E_{2}(z)]^{2}}.

Whenever a point zz in the upper-half plane ℌ\mathfrak H is a quadratic irrational number (namely, the minimal polynomial of zz has degree 22), both α4​(z)\alpha_{4}(z) and R−1/2(1−2α4(z))R_{-1/2}(1-2\alpha_{4}(z)) are explicitly computable algebraic numbers [69, §6].

    If we have either 2​z/i≥12z/i\geq 1, or Re⁡z=12\RE z=\frac{1}{2} and Im⁡z≥12\I z\geq\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}, then

    (1.21) Q1(z):⁣=∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​[𝖧2​k(2)−14​𝖧k(2)]​{α4​(z)​[1−α4​(z)]24}k∑k=0∞(2​kk)3​{α4​(z)​[1−α4​(z)]24}k=7​ζ​(3)4​π​Im⁡z−π2​[4​E​(z+12,2)−E⁡(2​z,2)]90−π2​i​[8​E4​(z+12)−E4​(2​z)]120​Im⁡z\displaystyle\begin{split}Q_{1}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}{}&\frac{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left[\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}-\frac{1}{4}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}\right]\left\{\frac{\alpha_{4}(z)[1-\alpha_{4}(z)]}{2^{4}}\right\}^{k}}{\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\binom{2k}{k}^{3}\left\{\frac{\alpha_{4}(z)[1-\alpha_{4}(z)]}{2^{4}}\right\}^{k}}\\ ={}&\frac{7\zeta(3)}{4\pi\I z}-\frac{\pi^{2}\left[4E\big(z+\frac{1}{2},2\big)-E(2z,2)\right]}{90}-\frac{\pi^{2}i\left[8E_{4}\big(z+\frac{1}{2}\big)-E_{4}(2z)\right]}{120\I z}\end{split}
    and

All the special values of Epstein zeta functions in Table 1 can be read off from [37, Table VI]. □\square

When zz is a quadratic irrational number listed in the first column of Table 1, there is a corresponding rational number r=r⁡(z)∈Qr=r(z)\in\mathbb Q, such that the sum

(1.26) Sr(z):⁣=7​ζ​(3)4​π​Im⁡z−π2​i​[8​E4​(z+12)−E4​(2​z)]120​Im⁡z+r⁡{2​π23​(Im⁡z)2+2​ζ​(3)π​Im⁡z+π2​i​[E4​(z+12)−2​E4​(2​z)]15​Im⁡z}\displaystyle\begin{split}S_{r}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}{}&\frac{7\zeta(3)}{4\pi\I z}-\frac{\pi^{2}i\left[8E_{4}\big(z+\frac{1}{2}\big)-E_{4}(2z)\right]}{120\I z}\\ {}&+r\left\{\frac{2\pi^{2}}{3}(\I z)^{2}+\frac{2\zeta(3)}{\pi\I z}+\frac{\pi^{2}i\left[E_{4}\big(z+\frac{1}{2}\big)-2E_{4}(2z)\right]}{15\I z}\right\}\end{split}

becomes a rational multiple of π2\pi^{2}, and that

(1.27) Tr(z):⁣=R1(z)−rR2(z)\displaystyle T_{r}(z)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}R_{1}(z)-rR_{2}(z)

The aforementioned property of Sr⁡(z)​(z)S_{r(z)}(z), together with the reductions of Epstein zeta functions to Dirichlet LL-values, allow us to prove (1.9)–(1.12) (cf. the penultimate column of Table 1), which have been recently conjectured by the first-named author in Question 507709 of MathOverflow [56]. Note that Eric Naslund has posted an answer to [56] that contained a complete proof of (1.9), but the more challenging identities (1.10)–(1.12) did not succumb to his method.

The corresponding property of Tr⁡(z)​(z)T_{r(z)}(z) (cf. the last column of Table 1) constitutes an alternative way to interpret (1.5)–(1.8). □\square

Inspired by the classical Ramanujan-type series (1.1)–(1.4) as well as their variants (1.5)–(1.8), the first-named author discovered the following identities [55, (90), (99), (104), (110)] experimentally:

In [66, §4], Wei and Xu verified (1.45) by hypergeometric transformations, extending Wei’s hypergeometric approach [60] to (1.8). However, such a hypergeometric method was not sharp enough to settle either (1.31) or (1.44) individually. □\square

In §4, we wrap up this article with discussions of some problems related to Theorem 1.1 and Theorem 1.2.

2. Infinite series involving (2​kk)3\binom{2k}{k}^{3}, 𝖧k(2)\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(2)}, and 𝖧2​k(2)\mathsf{H}_{2k}^{(2)}

In §2.1, we construct integral representations for our series of interest, by solving inhomogeneous differential equations. In §2.2, we introduce modular parametrizations for the series and their integral representations, thereby proving the main statements of Theorem 1.1. In §2.3, we study some special cases of Theorem 1.1, as listed in Table 1.

2.1. Second-order hypergeometric deformations and variation of parameters

Hereafter, we will use the following notation for a convergent generalized hypergeometric series

Fqp(a1,…,apb1,…,bq|t):=1+∑n=1∞∏j=1p(aj)n∏k=1q(bk)ntnn!,\displaystyle{{}_{p}F_{q}}\left(\left.\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}a_{1},\dots,a_{p}\\[4.0pt] b_{1},\dots,b_{q}\\ \end{array}\right|t\right):=1+\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{\prod_{j=1}^{p}(a_{j})_{n}}{\prod_{k=1}^{q}(b_{k})_{n}}\frac{t^{n}}{n!},

where (a)n:⁣=∏m=0n−1(a+m)(a)_{n}\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\prod_{m=0}^{n-1}(a+m) is the rising factorial, and b1,…,bqb_{1},\dots,b_{q} are neither zero nor negative integers. Occasionally, we will also write Fqp​(a1,…,apb1,…,bq|t){}_{p}F_{q}\left(\!\begin{smallmatrix}a_{1},\dots,a_{p}\\ b_{1},\dots,b_{q}\end{smallmatrix}\!\middle|t\right) for the analytic continuation of the convergent series defined above. For example, the complete elliptic integral of the first kind

𝐊(t):⁣=∫0π/2d⁡θ1−t​sin2⁡θ=π2F12(12,121|t)\displaystyle\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{t}\big)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\int_{0}^{\pi/2}\frac{\D\theta}{\sqrt{1-t\sin^{2}\theta}}=\frac{\pi}{2}{{}_{2}F_{1}}\left(\left.\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}\frac{1}{2},\frac{1}{2}\\[4.0pt] 1\\ \end{array}\right|t\right)

is defined for t∈C∖[1,∞)t\in\mathbb C\smallsetminus[1,\infty), whereas the corresponding hypergeometric series converges absolutely for |t|<1|t|<1.

When we talk about a ‘‘hypergeometric deformation’’, we refer to every possible (first-order or higher-order) partial derivative of a generalized hypergeometric series Fqp​(a1,…,apb1,…,bq|t){}_{p}F_{q}\left(\!\begin{smallmatrix}a_{1},\dots,a_{p}\\ b_{1},\dots,b_{q}\end{smallmatrix}\!\middle|t\right) with respect to its hypergeometric parameters a1,…,apa_{1},\dots,a_{p} and b1,…,bqb_{1},\dots,b_{q}. These hypergeometric deformations usually satisfy some inhomogeneous differential equations, which in turn, can be solved by a standard method called ‘‘variation of parameters’’. Such solutions lead to integral representations of certain hypergeometric deformations of our interest, as illustrated by the lemma below.

Lemma 2.1.

For |4​t​(1−t)|≤1|4t(1-t)|\leq 1 and Re⁡t≤12\RE t\leq\frac{1}{2}, we have the following integral representations for hypergeometric deformations:

Proof.

The first equalities in (2.5) and (2.6) are both consequences of termwise derivatives of the F23{}_{3}F_{2} series.

In §3.1, we upgrade the procedures of §2.1 to third-order partial derivatives with respect to the hypergeometric parameters, as well the integral representations that solve the corresponding inhomogeneous differential equations. In §3.2, we prove the main statements of Theorem 1.2, by introducing modular parametrizations to the integral representations constructed in §3.1. In §3.3, we study the special cases listed in Table 2.

3.1. Third-order hypergeometric deformations and variation of parameters

∂3∂ν2​∂εF34(1,1−ε,1−ε,1−ε32−ε,1−ν−ε,2+ν−ε|4t(1−t))|ν=−1/2ε=1/2,\displaystyle\left.\!\frac{\partial^{3}}{\partial\nu^{2}\partial\varepsilon}{{}_{4}F_{3}}\left(\left.\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}1,1-\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon,1-\varepsilon\\ \frac{3}{2}-\varepsilon,1-\nu-\varepsilon,2+\nu-\varepsilon\\ \end{array}\right|4t(1-t)\right)\right|_{\raisebox{2.3917pt}{$\begin{subarray}{c}\nu=-1/2\\ \varepsilon=1/2\hfill\end{subarray}$}},

which is equal to the left-hand side of (4.28). Now we apply the same differential operator to the right-hand side of (4.29) for |4​t​(1−t)|=1|4t(1-t)|=1. First, note that [cf. (3.22)]

(4.33) ∂3∂ν2​∂ε[−(1−2​ε)​(ν+ε)​(1+ν−ε)​T2​ε34F3(1,−ν+ε,1+ν+ε,12+ε1+ε,1+ε,1+ε|T)]|ν=−1/2ε=1/2=−(2π)2∫t∞4​(1−2​s)s⁡(1−s)[𝐊(1−s)𝐊(t)−𝐊(s)𝐊(1−t)]2ds\displaystyle\begin{split}&\left.\!\frac{\partial^{3}}{\partial\nu^{2}\partial\varepsilon}\left[-\frac{(1-2\varepsilon)(\nu+\varepsilon)(1+\nu-\varepsilon)T}{2\varepsilon^{3}}{{}_{4}F_{3}}\left(\left.\begin{array}[]{@{}c@{}}1,-\nu+\varepsilon,1+\nu+\varepsilon,\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon\\ 1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon,1+\varepsilon\\ \end{array}\right|T\right)\right]\right|_{\raisebox{2.3917pt}{$\begin{subarray}{c}\nu=-1/2\\ \varepsilon=1/2\hfill\end{subarray}$}}\\ ={}&-\left(\frac{2}{\pi}\right)^{2}\int_{t}^{\infty}\frac{4(1-2s)}{s(1-s)}\big[\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{\mathstrut 1-s}\big)\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{\mathstrut t}\big)-\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{\mathstrut s}\big)\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{\mathstrut 1-t}\big)\big]^{2}\D s\end{split}

enters the right-hand side of (4.28). Next, the third-order derivative of the remaining terms on the right-hand side of (4.29) are responsible for all the expressions involving T=14​t​(1−t)T=\frac{1}{4t(1-t)}.

Although the computations above depend on a constraint |4​t​(1−t)|=1|4t(1-t)|=1, the generic form of (4.28) follows readily from analytic continuation. ■\blacksquare

One may introduce modular parametrizations to (4.29), while observing that (cf. [30, pp. 38–40])

(4.34) 24​α4​(z)​[1−α4​(z)]​α4​(12​2​z−12​z+1)​[1−α4​(12​2​z−12​z+1)]=\displaystyle 2^{4}\alpha_{4}(z)[1-\alpha_{4}(z)]\alpha_{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{2z-1}{2z+1}\right)\left[1-\alpha_{4}\left(\frac{1}{2}\frac{2z-1}{2z+1}\right)\right]={} 1.\displaystyle 1.

The main lesson here is the following: even when the summands of our series are not as fine-tuned as those in Theorem 1.1 or Theorem 1.2, there may still be modularity lurking somewhere, though perhaps in a very sophisticated manner. □\square

4.3. A perspective on binomial harmonic sums

In recent years, the numerical experiments of the first-named author [54, 55, 57] have led to many conjectural closed forms for binomial harmonic sums in the form of

(4.35) ∑k=1∞(2​kk)Nks​(2​k−1)s′​(T22​N)k​[∏j=1M𝖧k(rj)]​[∏j′=1M′𝖧2​k(rj′′)],\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{\binom{2k}{k}^{N}}{k^{s}(2k-1)^{s^{\prime}}}\left(\frac{T}{2^{2N}}\right)^{k}\left[\prod_{j=1}^{M}\mathsf{H}_{k}^{(r_{j})}\right]\left[\prod_{\vphantom{j}\smash[b]{j^{\prime}}=1}^{M^{\prime}}{{\mathsf{H}}}_{\smash[t]{2}k}^{({r}^{\prime}_{j^{\prime}})}\right],

where N,s,s′∈ZN,s,s^{\prime}\in\mathbb Z, M,M′∈Z≥0M,M^{\prime}\in\mathbb Z_{\geq 0}, and |T|<1|T|<1.

The N∈{−1,0,1}N\in\{-1,0,1\} cases are pertinent to ε\varepsilon-expansions [namely, hypergeometric deformations of the Fqp{}_{p}F_{q} series defined in (2.1)] of quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics [1, 2, 4, 5, 6, 16, 18, 19, 33, 34, 45, 46, 67]. In [74, §3], binomial harmonic sums for N∈{−1,0,1}N\in\{-1,0,1\} are converted into linear combinations of contour integrals

(4.36) ∫CLia1,…,an⁡(z1​(t),…,zn​(t))​d⁡tR⁡(t),\displaystyle\int_{C}\Li_{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}}(z_{1}(t),\dots,z_{n}(t))\frac{\D t}{R(t)},

before their closed forms are found. Here in the integrand of (4.36), we have rational functions z1​(t),…,zn​(t)z_{1}(t),\dots,z_{n}(t), and R⁡(t)R(t), while Goncharov’s multiple polylogarithms (MPLs) [39, 40] are analytic continuations of the convergent series

(4.37) Lia1,…,an(z1,…,zn):⁣=∑ℓ1>⋯>ℓn>0∏j=1nzjℓjℓjaj\displaystyle\Li_{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}}(z_{1},\dots,z_{n})\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{\ell_{1}>\dots>\ell_{n}>0}\prod_{j=1}^{n}\frac{z_{j}^{\ell_{j}}}{\ell_{j}^{a_{j}}}

for certain a1,…,an∈Z>0a_{1},\dots,a_{n}\in\mathbb Z_{>0}. All these MPLs themselves arise from (iterated) integrals over products of logarithms and rational functions, such as

(4.38) ∫0zlog⁡(1−t)1−t​log​t​d​t=Li2,1⁡(z,1)−log2⁡(1−z)2​log​z\displaystyle\int_{0}^{z}\frac{\log(1-t)}{1-t}\log t\D t=\Li_{2,1}(z,1)-\frac{\log^{2}(1-z)}{2}\log z

for 0<|z|<10<|z|<1. Integrals over MPLs, like (4.36), are also expressible through a linear combination of MPLs, which in turn, leads to closed-form evaluation of (4.35) for N∈{−1,0,1}N\in\{-1,0,1\}. For z1=⋯=zn=1z_{1}=\dots=z_{n}=1 and a1≠1a_{1}\neq 1, the MPL Lia1,…,an⁡(z1,…,zn)\Li_{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}}(z_{1},\dots,z_{n}) becomes a multiple zeta value (MZV) ζa1,…,an\zeta_{a_{1},\dots,a_{n}}, which generalizes the Riemann zeta value ζ⁡(a)≡ζa\zeta(a)\equiv\zeta_{a} for a∈Z>1a\in\mathbb Z_{>1}. From a higher point of view, the MPLs and the MZVs are essentially motivic periods on the moduli spaces of genus-zero curves (namely, rational curves) [26, 27, 28].

If we have |N|>1|N|>1 in (4.35),88 8 For the borderline cases where T=1T=1 and N∈{−2,2}N\in\{-2,2\} in (4.35), one is still dealing with rational curves instead of elliptic curves. The corresponding series have been already covered by the methods in [74, §3]. then we are obliged to cope with the moduli spaces of genus-one curves (namely, elliptic curves), in which the complete elliptic integrals 𝐊⁡(t)\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{t}) and 𝐊⁡(1−t)\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{1-t}\big) take the places of log⁡t\log t and log⁡(1−t)\log(1-t). There is a wealth of literature on genus-one analogs of MZVs/MPLs, namely elliptic multiple zeta values (EMZVs) [24, 25, 35, 36, 38, 49, 50, 70] and elliptic multiple polylogarithms (EMPLs) [3, 7, 8, 9, 17, 20, 22, 21, 23, 29, 53, 68], with diverse notational conventions. In one of these notational systems (see [3, 7, 8, 23], for example), the elliptic polylogarithm is defined as

(4.39) ELin;m(x;y;q):⁣=∑j=1∞∑k=1∞xj​ykjn​kmqj​k=∑j=1∞xjjnLim(yqj)=∑k=1∞ykkmLin(xqk).\displaystyle\ELi_{n;m}(x;y;q)\mathrel{\mathchoice{\vbox{\hbox{$\displaystyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\textstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptstyle:$}}}{\vbox{\hbox{$\scriptscriptstyle:$}}}{=}}\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^{j}y^{k}}{j^{n}k^{m}}q^{jk}=\sum_{j=1}^{\infty}\frac{x^{j}}{j^{n}}\Li_{m}\big(yq^{j}\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{y^{k}}{k^{m}}\Li_{n}\big(xq^{k}\big).

This definition not only echoes (4.37), but also embodies the Lambert–Ramanujan series

(4.40) ELi0;m⁡(1,1,q)=\displaystyle\ELi_{0;m}(1;1;q)={} ∑k=1∞1km​qk1−qk\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{\infty}\frac{1}{k^{m}}\frac{q^{k}}{1-q^{k}}

as a special case. Since we have

(4.41) ∑k=0∞(−1)k(2​k+1)2​1q−2​k−1−1=8​ELi0;2​(1,i,q)+2​ELi0;2​(1,1,q2)−ELi0;2⁡(1,1,q4)8​i,\displaystyle\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^{k}}{(2k+1)^{2}}\frac{1}{q^{-2k-1}-1}=\frac{8\ELi_{0;2}(1;i;q)+2\ELi_{0;2}(1;1;q^{2})-\ELi_{0;2}(1;1;q^{4})}{8i},

the right-hand side of (4.16) can be expressed in terms of elliptic polylogarithms. It appears that for generic settings of (4.35) with |N|>1|N|>1, one cannot reduce the corresponding elliptic polylogarithms [cf. (4.15) and (4.21)] to familiar arithmetic objects like Eichler integrals.

According to [75] and the current work, each provable evaluation of (4.35) for N∈{−3,2,3}N\in\{-3,2,3\} invokes a product of at least |N|−1|N|-1 elliptic integrals (either in isolation or as part of an integrand). It is possible to derive closed-form evaluations for certain integrals over the products of four or more elliptic integrals, such as (cf. [58, Table 1], [72, (4.18)–(4.19)], and [73, (1.1)])

(4.42) ζ⁡(5)=\displaystyle\zeta(5)={} 893​∫01(1−2​t)​[𝐊⁡(1−t)]4​d⁡t,\displaystyle\frac{8}{93}\int_{0}^{1}(1-2t)\big[\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{1-t}\big)\big]^{4}\D t,
(4.43) ζ⁡(7)=\displaystyle\zeta(7)={} 325715​∫01[2−17​t​(1−t)]​[𝐊⁡(1−t)]6​d⁡t.\displaystyle\frac{32}{5715}\int_{0}^{1}[2-17t(1-t)]\big[\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{1-t}\big)\big]^{6}\D t.

More generally, some special values of the Epstein zeta functions E⁡(z,s)E(z,s) and the Dirichlet LL-functions Ld​(s)L_{d}(s) (where s∈Z>1s\in\mathbb Z_{>1}) can be represented by integrals whose integrands involve products of 2​(s−1)2(s-1) complete elliptic integrals, such as (cf. [72, (4.29)])

(4.44) 105​L−4​(4)136​π4=200025​ζ​(7)2176​π7−70136​π7​∫01/2[2−17​t​(1−t)]​[𝐊⁡(t)]6​{[𝐊⁡(1−t)𝐊⁡(t)]2−1}3​d⁡t.\displaystyle\begin{split}&\frac{105L_{-4}(4)}{136\pi^{4}}\\ ={}&\frac{200025\zeta(7)}{2176\pi^{7}}-\frac{70}{136\pi^{7}}\int_{0}^{1/2}[2-17t(1-t)]\big[\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{t}\big)\big]^{6}\left\{\left[\frac{\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{1-t}\big)}{\mathbf{K}\big(\sqrt{t}\big)}\right]^{2}-1\right\}^{3}\D t.\end{split}

Will these integral formulae shed new light99 9 Some individual cases of (4.35) for N∈{−7,−5,5,7}N\in\{-7,-5,5,7\} have already been tackled combinatorially [10, 11, 44, 60, 61, 63, 65]. As for “new light”, we are expecting modular parametrizations similar to the current work. on (4.35) for N∈{−7,−5,5,7}N\in\{-7,-5,5,7\}? Maybe we will see the answer in the near future.
